narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 24, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that this was the main reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.30 it is slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore helped pull the prediction back toward passing, though not enough to overcome the LSAT impact.

Your third-year class ranking also nudged the outcome slightly toward success. Being in the fourth decile is only modestly below the 5.79 average of accepted students, so this factor offered some positive signal but carried less weight than the LSAT.

In short, the low LSAT score outweighed your solid grades and slightly better-than-average college performance. To improve your chances, you should focus on retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score before reapplying. This single change would likely shift the model’s outlook and open the door to admission. (218 words)
